items.question: Why do you see learning from the robot’s own experience as a significant change in Pi Star 0.6?
items.object: Reinforcement learning from robot experience in Pi Star 0.6
items.answer: I think the main difference, if we want to contrast it to what we talked about earlier, is that up to that point basically all of the robotics foundational model learning that we've done was demonstration data, teleoperated going into the model. The model is trained kind of like just imitate that data, right? And now with this new model Pi Star 6, what we're using is RL from experience that the robot collects itself by actually running a policy. So we start with the initial policy, this demonstration-trained policy, and then you deploy it. You try to actually have the robot solve the task, and then it additionally gets reward signals given by humans, and it can also get correction, where the human intervenes and says, “Oh, actually, you know what, this is not right. Let's do this a little differently.” And that data is collected, comes back in, and the model kind of uses that data to try and figure out which of the data should I reinforce, should I do more of, and which do I do less of, and basically improve itself over time. That's kind of the big distinction, and having that stream of real data coming in is the missing piece that Karol was talking about that allows us to now escape this plateau that otherwise we were finding we were getting to.

rubrics.text: The response identifies Pi Star 0.6’s central change as a shift from imitating teleoperated demonstrations to reinforcement learning from experience the robot collects by executing its own policy.
The response identifies an ongoing stream of robot-collected real-world experience as the missing input that enables learning to overcome the previous performance plateau.

items.question: What impressed you most about Pi Star 0.6’s results after reinforcement learning?
items.object: Pi Star 0.6’s real-world reinforcement learning results
items.answer:
I think for me the most impressive thing, honestly, personally, to see was just having these models run for hours at a time, recover from lots of different failures, and basically just keep going, and at the same time do that at a rate that is much better than the initial model that we started with. The headline figures were we increased the throughput of the policies by over 2x on these three tasks. One task was this box-building task I already talked about. One was making coffee with an actual industrial-scale espresso machine, and the other one was folding laundry.

For each of them we managed to make the base policy that was trained just from demonstrations much faster and also make it able to recover from failures much better. Seeing that in action, when you sit there—we have, if you go to our website, you can look at the videos—we have the robot serve coffee for 13 hours in a row or fold laundry for four hours, things like that. Actually seeing that live changes the way you think about these models.

items.question: How do you see reinforcement learning contributing to both deployment reliability and new capabilities in general-purpose robots?
items.answer:
I think it's both. To some extent the robots that we really want, the robot that you want at home which can do your laundry, do your dishes, cook for you, drive around, and also the robot that people want in these smaller businesses, maybe solving a real problem that they have that they don't want to automate in a classical way because it's too expensive, like building a chocolate box, those are things where the robot has to be reliable, has to be good, and it has to have the capability to do a new task that it hasn't seen in initial training stages. I think it's unrealistic for us to assume that we can just go with more and more human data collection, go bigger, bigger, bigger. We will do that, but there is always going to be a limit to how good and how much data you can get and how good the initial policy is going to be. So I think it is what you said: if we want deployments, we need this. But also, increasingly over the next years, I expect we will see that we will do these deployments and that data will actually become really valuable as a source for pre-training, for making our models better themselves. And we'll rely more and more on autonomous data collection, is my prediction, over the next coming years, to build that host of data, that convex hull of all the tasks that we want robots eventually to do, such that the models ingest this and become good at doing them and interpolating.

And I think of it as a new capability. We haven't so far figured out how to learn from your own experience, or there have been many attempts, but I don't think we've seen it done at scale to the extent that it actually shows a convincing result that allows you to deploy something.

rubrics.text: The response argues that scaling human-collected training data alone cannot indefinitely improve robots’ initial policies.
The response predicts that data collected during robot deployments will become a valuable source of pre-training data.
The response predicts increasing reliance on autonomous data collection to build robot training datasets.
The response states that learning from robots’ own experience has not yet been demonstrated at a scale that convincingly supports deployment.

items.question: Why do you think it matters for robots to learn from their own experience?
items.object: Robots learning from their own experience
items.answer: You need to try the thing yourself. You need to see how your actions impact what you actually want to achieve, and make your own conclusions and try to learn that way. And I think this is the first step towards that.
quotes: You need to try the thing yourself. You need to see how your actions impact what you actually want to achieve, and make your own conclusions and try to learn that way. And I think this is the first step towards that.

rubrics.text: The response explains that firsthand experience lets robots observe how their own actions affect achievement of their goals.

items.question: How do you assess whether robots that keep learning from experience after deployment qualify as continual learning?
items.object: Continual learning in robotics through deployment and experience
items.answer:
It kind of depends what people mean by continual learning. I think it's definitely more continual than what we've done in the past, where you have a big pre-training mixture and maybe a post-training mixture, and you sit down, work really hard, and then you come up with an artifact and that's it. Now this is much more of a living thing, right? We start with a process similar to this, but then you deploy it and then it keeps on learning.

So it's much more continual in that sense, that it tries new things. It tries to learn from its own experience and it keeps on getting better. Now, I think there is still room for it to be much more continual, where it can acquire new skills that way or it can be even much faster in doing this. It can probably reason throughout this process. So I think there's a spectrum of how much you can learn on the job, and this is really promising because it shows that you can do it, but I think we can make it much better.
